cards.body: University learning works differently from school or college. Here you are joining a discourse community — the people who study, argue about and build the knowledge of your subject. This lesson introduces that idea and why it changes how you read, write and use feedback.
You are at the start of your degree, so these ways of working are new — and that is exactly where you should be. Nothing below assumes you have done this before; we build from first principles.

cards.displayTitle: What you will be able to do
cards.body:
• Describe what a discourse community is.
  • Recognise how it shapes a tutor's expectations.
  • Identify one convention of your own subject.

A discourse community is a group of people brought together by a shared interest in a subject, who together create and develop that subject's ideas — its discourse (Swales, 1990). At university you are joining one. Learning, here, means gradually taking part in that community's way of thinking, talking and writing.

cards.displayTitle: What it looks like in practice
cards.body: A discourse community shows up as the habits of a subject: how a historian weighs a source, how a psychologist reports a study, how an engineer justifies a design. These are not arbitrary rules — they are how the community checks and builds knowledge, and they are the conventions your tutors expect you to meet.

Think of a time you were told to write or present “in the right way” for a subject — referencing a certain way, or structuring an argument a certain way. That instruction was the discourse community's conventions at work. Hold that example in mind as you read on.

Weaker: “I think the book was good and I agree with it.”

Stronger: “The author's claim is persuasive because it is supported by three studies; a reader might still question whether it holds outside the UK.”

The stronger version does what the community values: it gives reasons, points to evidence, and leaves room for debate.

items.text: When set a task, ask: what does this subject count as a good answer?
Notice how your reading lists write — copy the moves, not the words.
Treat tutor feedback as the community showing you its conventions.
A social club for students on the same course
A group who share a subject and together build its knowledge and ways of working

feedback.correct: Yes — it is the people and practices that create and develop a subject's knowledge.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite — think about who creates and develops a subject's ideas. Try again.
feedback.final: The key idea is a shared subject and shared ways of building its knowledge.

questions.body: Why do subjects have different conventions for writing and arguing?

items.text: To make study harder for new students
Because the conventions are how each community checks and builds knowledge
They are set centrally by the university for every subject

feedback.correct: Right — conventions carry the community's way of testing ideas.
feedback.incorrect: Have another go — think about what the conventions are for.
feedback.final: Conventions exist because they are how the community checks and builds knowledge.

questions.body: Where would you most likely see your subject's conventions?

items.text: In how your reading lists are written and how feedback is phrased

feedback.correct: Yes — the conventions are visible in the community's own writing and in tutor feedback.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite — where does the community's writing actually appear? Try again.
feedback.final: You see the conventions in the subject's writing and in the feedback you receive.

cards.body: Think of your subject. What is one “way of working” — a habit of reading, writing or arguing — you have already noticed that feels specific to it? Note it down. This is private and unmarked.

• Learning at university means joining a discourse community.
  • Its conventions are how the community builds and checks knowledge.
  • You meet those conventions in your reading and in tutor feedback.

Next: how tutors design learning around this.
